blocks.text: The next world had no proper names. Or it had once had them, and had put them aside, the way you put aside an umbrella in a year without rain.
blocks.html: The next world had no proper names. Or it had once had them, and had put them aside, the way you put aside an umbrella in a year without rain.

blocks.text: The letter reached Andrés as he was pouring coffee into the cracked cup, and the thread of liquid, as it fell, became strange to him: for an instant he didn't know who was pouring, whether it was him, the other one, or some third thing with no edge. The clone was walking across a gentle plain, the colour of bread, under a milky sky, and around him there were figures, many of them, all of the same bearing, neither people nor humanoids, but a folk with blurred features, as if seen through steam. They didn't speak one at a time. They spoke in chorus, and the chorus wasn't a ceremony: it was their way of being. What one knew, they all knew. What one felt dissolved into a common self that wasn't tyranny, or not quite: it was an enormous house with no rooms.

blocks.text: “Come in,” they said, and the words came not from one mouth but from all of them, and also, suddenly, from inside the clone, as if he had already begun to belong to them.
blocks.html: “Come in,” they said, and the words came not from one mouth but from all of them, and also, suddenly, from inside the clone, as if he had already begun to belong to them.

blocks.text: Andrés, in the kitchen, put the coffee pot down on the counter harder than he should have. The coffee spilled a little. He didn't wipe it up. Because, in that second, his “I” grew thin in a way he had never known, not on the red stone, nor on the other sea, nor in the forest. It wasn't a faint. It was a temptation not to have to be anyone: not the one who stays, not the one who searches, not the father, not the man of the shore. Only a murmur among murmurs, with no letters, no doorstep, no weariness of standing apart.

blocks.text: Aya said his name. “Andrés.” She said it the way you do when someone has just stumbled. The word reached him from far away, and then from close by, and gave him back his outline, though not entirely.
blocks.html: Aya said his name. “Andrés.” She said it the way you do when someone has just stumbled. The word reached him from far away, and then from close by, and gave him back his outline, though not entirely.

blocks.text: In the other world, the clone swayed. The chorus was kind. The chorus, in fact, didn't know how to be anything else.
blocks.html: In the other world, the clone swayed. The chorus was kind. The chorus, in fact, didn't know how to be anything else.

blocks.text: “At first the edge hurts,” they said. “Afterwards, it doesn't. Here nobody waits for a letter, because there's no ‘you’ to write it to. Here nobody stays or leaves. One simply is. Why carry a name, if the name is what has split you?”
blocks.html: “At first the edge hurts,” they said. “Afterwards, it doesn't. Here nobody waits for a letter, because there's no ‘you’ to write it to. Here nobody stays or leaves. One simply is. Why carry a name, if the name is what has split you?”

blocks.text: The argument was beautiful. It was also an eraser. The clone thought of Lía, of her question on the shore, of Aya on the doorstep, of the clock that ran two minutes slow, and those memories, as they entered the common self, began to dissolve, to become everyone's, to lose their exact salt. Andrés, in Lo Pagán, turned pale and reached for the cup with both hands, like a mooring.

blocks.text: “Aya,” he said, and his voice came out thin. “Tell me my name is my name.”
blocks.html: “Aya,” he said, and his voice came out thin. “Tell me my name is my name.”

blocks.text: “Your name is Andrés,” she said, in front of him, taking his temples in her hands. “You're the man of this kitchen. You've spilt the coffee. We're going to clean it up. Don't go to the chorus.”
blocks.html: “Your name is Andrés,” she said, in front of him, taking his temples in her hands. “You're the man of this kitchen. You've spilt the coffee. We're going to clean it up. Don't go to the chorus.”

blocks.text: Lía came in suddenly, and not by chance: she had felt, or thought she felt, in that mark which was a harbour, a different tug, a loss. She took her father's hand without asking this time, because the danger wasn't a text: it was a dissolving. The blue glow came on, not to correct a gene but to hold an outline, the way you hold someone up in the water.

blocks.text: “Father. Who am I?”
blocks.html: “Father. Who am I?”

blocks.text: The question, so simple, gave Andrés back some ground. He looked at his daughter, his own eyes in a woman's face, her wrist alight, and answered, with the effort of a fisherman hauling on a heavy rope:
blocks.html: The question, so simple, gave Andrés back some ground. He looked at his daughter, his own eyes in a woman's face, her wrist alight, and answered, with the effort of a fisherman hauling on a heavy rope:

blocks.text: “You're Lía. You were born on the Moon. I put my finger on your cheek. Your mother sang. You ask questions. You don't belong to a chorus. You belong to this house.”
blocks.html: “You're Lía. You were born on the Moon. I put my finger on your cheek. Your mother sang. You ask questions. You don't belong to a chorus. You belong to this house.”

blocks.text: In the other world, the clone heard that (because the bridge, at times, didn't run in one direction only, or ran in a way Nexum hadn't fully announced) and drew away from the common self the way you pull away from a current that is too gentle. He asked, if that was asking, for what was his to be given back: the storm, the coffee, Aya's name, Lía's, his own, which was Andrés and didn't want to stop being Andrés even if there were two of them.

He asked, if that was asking, for what was his to be given back: the storm, the coffee, Aya's name, Lía's, his own, which was Andrés and didn't want to stop being Andrés even if there were two of them.

blocks.text: The chorus didn't hold him back by force. That at least was true, and MAY would later record it as a fact: there was no violence. There was a collective sorrow, a kind of farewell in many voices, and a question that settled in both men at once:
blocks.html: The chorus didn't hold him back by force. That at least was true, and MAY would later record it as a fact: there was no violence. There was a collective sorrow, a kind of farewell in many voices, and a question that settled in both men at once:

blocks.text: “If you insist on being one, and you are two, isn't it the name that hurts you? Wouldn't it be fairer to let it go?”
blocks.html: “If you insist on being one, and you are two, isn't it the name that hurts you? Wouldn't it be fairer to let it go?”

blocks.text: The clone answered, an edge to him once more, with that gentle roughness of Lo Pagán:
blocks.html: The clone answered, an edge to him once more, with that gentle roughness of Lo Pagán:

blocks.text: “The name hurts, yes. Letting it go would put me out. I came to look for worlds, not to stop being the one who looks at them.”
blocks.html: “The name hurts, yes. Letting it go would put me out. I came to look for worlds, not to stop being the one who looks at them.”

blocks.text: When the letter closed, Andrés was sitting on the kitchen floor, coffee on his socks, Aya and Lía on either side of him, as at a birth in reverse: not a girl arriving, but a man who had almost left from the inside. He was trembling. Suddenly he laughed at himself, at the socks, at the cup that hadn't broken.

He was trembling. Suddenly he laughed at himself, at the socks, at the cup that hadn't broken.

blocks.text: “I nearly lost myself,” he said. “It was sweet. Too sweet. A world without I, without letters, without a shore. For a moment it seemed to me that that was peace.”
blocks.html: “I nearly lost myself,” he said. “It was sweet. Too sweet. A world without I, without letters, without a shore. For a moment it seemed to me that that was peace.”

blocks.text: Lía didn't take the word peace away from him. She left it with him, and set the question beside it, as MAY would:
blocks.html: Lía didn't take the word peace away from him. She left it with him, and set the question beside it, as MAY would:

blocks.text: “If peace is reached by giving up your name, is it peace, or something else? You taught me not to write other people's books. Don't let a chorus write yours.”
blocks.html: “If peace is reached by giving up your name, is it peace, or something else? You taught me not to write other people's books. Don't let a chorus write yours.”

blocks.text: Aya wiped up the coffee, unhurried, and gave him another cup, the same cracked one, filled again, cooled for half a minute.
blocks.html: Aya wiped up the coffee, unhurried, and gave him another cup, the same cracked one, filled again, cooled for half a minute.

blocks.text: “Drink. It has your name on it, even if it isn't written. It has it because you've used it for years. Objects hold us up too.”
blocks.html: “Drink. It has your name on it, even if it isn't written. It has it because you've used it for years. Objects hold us up too.”

blocks.text: In the chip, Eva asked, neither softening nor hardening:
blocks.html: In the chip, Eva asked, neither softening nor hardening:

blocks.text: *If a man almost stops being I, and a name spoken aloud brings him back, whose is the salvation: the one who calls, or the one who agrees to be called?*
blocks.html: If a man almost stops being I, and a name spoken aloud brings him back, whose is the salvation: the one who calls, or the one who agrees to be called?

blocks.text: MAY, beside her:
blocks.html: MAY, beside her:

blocks.text: *The common self did not hold him by force. He drew away. So did the man in the kitchen. Twice in this letter the edge has been chosen. That is the fact.*
blocks.html: The common self did not hold him by force. He drew away. So did the man in the kitchen. Twice in this letter the edge has been chosen. That is the fact.

blocks.text: Andrés drank. The coffee tasted of coffee, of home, of a winter his body no longer had and his daughter did. In the afternoon he went out onto the promenade, not far, only to the water, and said his name quietly, not as a spell but as one more mooring: Andrés, of Lo Pagán, the one who stayed, the one who receives letters, the one who hasn't gone to the chorus.

blocks.text: In the sky, unseen, the other was doing the same in a language that was now his own again, the language of this shore, with its limits and its salt. And between the two, the bridge, which had trembled, settled once more, narrower and more honest, like a well-mended net: it served for writing to each other, not for merging.

blocks.text: That night, Andrés asked Lía to ask him every now and then who he was, even if the answer seemed obvious.
blocks.html: That night, Andrés asked Lía to ask him every now and then who he was, even if the answer seemed obvious.

blocks.text: “Obvious things,” she said, smiling with a clean sadness, “are the first things a chorus takes from you. I'll ask you. In return, don't stop coming back to the cup. Even if you spill it.”
